### 2026-10-07 – At the beginning of the week, I learned how to make PCBs. To do this, I followed 2 tutorials, and created 2 circuit boards from scratch. The first one was easier and a video tutorial, and the second w

**4h**

At the beginning of the week, I learned how to make PCBs. To do this, I followed 2 tutorials, and created 2 circuit boards from scratch. The first one was easier and a video tutorial, and the second was more complex, and just a text tutorial. The first used a wireless module to turn on an LED. The second took power input from a USB-C female connector and powered an LED with a switch. I turned both of these into PCB designs and laid out the board, and also routed them. This took me about an hour.

Having learned how to make PCBs, I then began copying the schematic for the microphone PCB onto EasyEDA, ready to be laid out onto the PCB.

However, unfortunately, I have decided that my original project idea of a microphone was just too hard. So, I'm going for 5 simple projects instead. Today, I planned out and designed my MIDI keyboard that I'm going to make using cherry MX switches.
Once I had created a design and a plan, I began to make the schematic, loosely following this hack club tutorial: https://blueprint.hackclub.com/starter-projects/midi
I am going to have 25 keys, octave up and down keys, 2 rotary encoders for modulation, and a pitch bend wheel. I added all these to my PCB schematic. Tomorrow, I can turn it into a PCB!

### 2026-10-08 – Today I finished off designing the schematic. Turns out there were quite a few issues with it! So I think I have fixed those now. I have also made some decisions about how this is going to work.

**1.2h**

Today I finished off designing the schematic. Turns out there were quite a few issues with it! So I think I have fixed those now. I have also made some decisions about how this is going to work.
I'm going with a 1 octave, 9-key keyboard like your computer keys in a DAW. This is because the PCB would be crazy expensive if I went with a standard 25 keys. So I'll just stick to one and make this mini and cute 😂.
So, I just need to modify the key matrix to only have 15 switches, plus 2 for the rotary encoder switches. Then I can lay out the PCB! Hooray!

### 2026-10-08 – I guess going into this with very little plan wasn't the greatest idea of all time...

**1.2h**

I guess going into this with very little plan wasn't the greatest idea of all time...
Looking at the budget, making a full 25 keys was just too expensive. Long PCBs are CRAZY expensive. And since I'm only going for 9 white keys and 6 black, I no longer have more keys than GPIO pins on the pi pico. In fact, I have more pins that keys now! So, considering my ameteur-ishness, I've decided to forget the matrix idea. It would have probably worked, but there's a good chance it just didn't. Instead, I'll just wire the switches straight into the pico. Which is probably more reliable for a keyboard anyway now that I think about it. So, after trimming my matrix down to a 4x4 to save on board size, I have now done away with it altogether and switched to a simpler direct connection design. I've laid out the switches and found the footprint I'll need to use (oh and made modifications to the pico's connections). So I just need to finish wiring those up and hopefully, after a round of verification, I should be good to get going with the actual PCB layout!

### 2026-10-09 – Have you SEEN how much a long PCB costs??!!

**1.23h**

Have you SEEN how much a long PCB costs??!!
(well anything over 100x100mm)

So I am pivoting again. Only a small pivot this time, though. Guess I win the prize for most pivots? (probably not lol)

I am still making a MIDI Controller MacroPad. But instead of it being a MIDI keyboard, it's going to be a 'transport controller' instead for Ableton, my music software of choice (a DAW). So it will output MIDI signals and Ableton will read those as signals to record, or play, or solo a track, or undo, etc etc. One rotary encoder will scroll sideways through the timeline, and the other will zoom in/zoom out. Then, a toggle button will be able to switch between apps, and send keyboard signals instead. Or both at once for cmd+z to undo. 3/4 LEDs will give a binary output of the number of the app mode I am in.

### 2026-10-10 – Okay, I am almost there! I have fully designed the PCB today!

**2.7h**

Okay, I am almost there! I have fully designed the PCB today!

I finalised the schematic, putting in the final components like the LEDs, and connecting all the exact components from LCSC. That way all the footprints are automatically correct! I love you EasyEDA LCSC integration.

Then, I moved onto the PCB design. First came laying out all the components. I thought that was hard, but little did I know...
Anyway, I got a layout I was happy with (it's almost the same as my drawing - just had to move the knobs up to the top and the mode switch under the macro keys. Not exactly where I wanted it, but it will be under my hand, since the bottom right key will always be space to play/pause.

Then came routing the traces. Oh man. This took FOREVER. The temptation to hit 'Auto-Route' was real, but I resisted and laid it all out myself. Probably the most disgusting routing ever seen, but there we go. No DRC errors first try! Just got to hope all those vias are fine.

Connecting all the ground pins to a copper area was a pretty neat way to ground it all and I love how the area wraps around the traces without interrupting them! So cool.

A bit of silkscreen designing, adding my logo and a little message under where the pi will sit, and I think the PCB is pretty much done!

### 2026-10-11 – BOOM! I think my project is now done!

**2.2h**

BOOM! I think my project is now done!

I started today by deciding to move to brown switches, so they have more of a tactile feedback effect when pressed, but aren't loud like blues. Shouldn't be much louder than reds.

Then, I moved onto firmware. I am pretty good at Python (I would say advanced perhaps?!) but have never used CircuitPython before, so I had a lot of learning to do! I settled on CircuitPython and KMK to program the firmware. KMK provides pretty much every bit of functionality I wanted, so all I had to do was figure out how to implement all the logic I wanted.

After a good bit of learning and programming, I am pleased to say that the firmware is done, and hopefully working! And with that, the project should be done too! Just got to update my BOM for the final time, then submit the project!
